title: King Wu's Speech at Mu
speaker: King Wu of Zhou
place: Muye, near the Shang capital Yin
before: King Wu of Zhou, leading his own people and a coalition of allied states against Di Xin, the last Shang king, addressed his army at dawn on the plain of Muye before the battle. The speech, the Oath at Muye, is recorded in the Book of Documents. The accounts of the conquest come from the victorious Zhou and their successors, and its charges against Di Xin are not borne out by the oracle bones of his reign.
excerpt: Now, I, Fâ, am simply executing respectfully the punishment appointed by Heaven.
source: Book of Documents, Part V, Book II, tr. James Legge, Sacred Books of the East, vol. 3 (1879). Fâ is the king's personal name; Shâu is Di Xin.
after: Many of the Shang soldiers fled or went over to the Zhou, and the Shang army was destroyed. In the traditional account Di Xin set fire to his Deer Terrace Pavilion and died inside it. The victory ended the Shang and founded the Zhou dynasty, and Chinese historians held it up as an example of the Mandate of Heaven passing from one dynasty to another. King Wu died about three years later.
notes: The imported text keeps Legge's section numbers ("1.", "2.") and two footnote asterisks (after "received)" and after "Heaven."): a $FIXES entry could drop the asterisks. c. 1046 BCE is the Xia-Shang-Zhou Chronology Project's date; the Battle of Muye article notes at least 44 proposed dates (1130-1018 BCE).

title: The Buddha's First Sermon
speaker: Gautama Buddha
place: The deer park at Isipatana (Sarnath), near Varanasi
before: According to Buddhist tradition, seven weeks after his enlightenment under the Bodhi Tree at Bodh Gaya, the Buddha went to the deer park at Isipatana, near Varanasi, to find the five ascetics who had shared six years of hardship with him. They suspected at first that he had given up the search. He persuaded them to listen and set out the Middle Way between indulgence and self-mortification, and the Four Noble Truths.
excerpt: There is a middle path, Bhikkhus, avoiding these two extremes, discovered by the Tathagata (Buddha), a path which opens the eyes and bestows understanding, which leads to peace of mind, to the higher wisdom, to full enlightenment, to Nirvana!
source: Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, the opening as quoted by Romesh Chunder Dutt, History of India, vol. 1 (1906). The sutta was handed down orally for centuries; scholars doubt how much of it the Buddha said.
after: In the sutta's account Kondañña, one of the five, understood the teaching as he listened and became the first of the Buddha's disciples to awaken. The compilers of the Canon put into it what they held to be the essence of his awakening, and in central Thailand stone wheels of the law of the Dvaravati period were carved with its passage on the four truths, about a thousand years before the oldest surviving Pali manuscripts.
notes: No clean free full text was found. Rhys Davids's translation (Sacred Books of the East 11, 1881) is on Wikisource only as an untranscribed scan; sacred-texts.com refuses automated requests; archive.org has only OCR with footnote marks and broken words. Dutt prints the opening only (the two extremes and the middle path, 107 words): his wording follows Rhys Davids's closely but not exactly ("unworthy" for "ignoble", his gloss "(Buddha)" after Tathagata). The articles give no date: c. 5th century BCE is the encyclopedia's own date for the Buddha ("around the fifth century BCE"); year -450 only places it in that century. No profile for the kingdom it was spoken in is alive then, so empire is empty.

title: Alcibiades for the Sicilian Expedition
speaker: Alcibiades
before: In 415 BCE envoys from Segesta asked Athens for help in a war with Selinus, and the Assembly voted sixty ships under Nicias, Alcibiades and Lamachus. Five days later, at a second assembly, Nicias tried to have the decision reversed and attacked Alcibiades as a young man eager to lead the city into war for his own ends. Alcibiades replied. The speech is known from the History of Thucydides, who wrote it in his own words.
excerpt: And we cannot fix the exact point at which our empire shall stop; we have reached a position in which we must not be content with retaining but must scheme to extend it, for, if we cease to rule others, we are in danger of being ruled ourselves.
source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War, VI.16-18, tr. Richard Crawley (1874). The words are Thucydides' composition, not a record of what Alcibiades said.
after: The Assembly leaned his way; when Nicias, hoping to deter it, said a far larger force was needed, it voted over 100 ships and 5,000 hoplites. After the hermai were mutilated, Alcibiades was recalled from Sicily to stand trial, escaped at Thurii and went over to Sparta, which he advised to fortify Decelea. The expedition ended in 413 BCE with nearly the whole force killed, captured or enslaved.

title: Cato on the Oppian Law
speaker: Cato the Elder
before: The Oppian law, passed in 215 BCE after the defeat at Cannae, forbade women to own more than half an ounce of gold, wear multicoloured garments or ride in carriages in the city. In 195 BCE, the war won, the tribunes Marcus Fundanius and Lucius Valerius moved its repeal, and the matrons of Rome filled the streets and the approaches to the Forum. The consul Cato spoke against them. Livy gives the speech in his own words.
excerpt: If you allow them to pull away these restraints and wrench them out one after another, and finally put themselves on an equality with their husbands, do you imagine that you will be able to tolerate them? From the moment that they become your fellows they will become your masters.
source: Livy, Ab Urbe Condita XXXIV.2-4, tr. Canon Roberts (1905). The speech is Livy's own composition, not a record of Cato's words.
after: Lucius Valerius answered that the law had been a temporary measure of the war. The next day the women came out in greater numbers and besieged the doors of the two Brutuses, the tribunes who opposed repeal; they gave way, and the Oppian law was repealed by the vote of all the tribes. Cato soon sailed for his province, Hispania Citerior.
notes: The two articles disagree on the law's proposer (Marcus or Gaius Oppius) and on the second Brutus (Publius or Titus), so neither is named. The Lex Oppia article gives the reply to the consul Flaccus in one sentence and to Lucius Valerius in the next; in Livy the reply is the tribune's, so the record says only 'Lucius Valerius'.

title: Tiberius Gracchus on the Landless
speaker: Tiberius Gracchus
before: Elected tribune of the plebs for 133 BCE, Tiberius Gracchus proposed a law to enforce the old limit on holdings of public land and hand the surplus to poor citizens; the traditional accounts said rich men held it as large estates worked by slaves, which had displaced poorer farmers. To the crowds round the speakers' platform he spoke for the landless soldiers. Plutarch reports the speech in brief, long afterwards.
excerpt: They fought indeed, and were slain, but it was to maintain the luxury and the wealth of other men. They were styled the masters of the world, but in the meantime had not one foot of ground which they could call their own.
source: Plutarch, Life of Tiberius Gracchus 9, tr. John Warren in the Dryden translation revised by Arthur Hugh Clough (1859). Plutarch quotes a sentence and summarises the rest.
after: The senate set his fellow tribune Marcus Octavius to veto the bill; Tiberius had him removed from office, and the law passed. When he stood for re-election, the pontifex maximus Scipio Nasica led a mob to the voting on the Capitol, where Tiberius and his supporters were beaten to death and thrown into the Tiber. The land commission carried on, and his death is taken as the start of the Republic's crisis.
notes: The imported text is the passage of chapter 9 from the speech's first words to the end of Plutarch's summary (173 words); Plutarch gives only the opening as direct speech.

title: Caesar on the Catilinarian Conspirators
speaker: Julius Caesar
before: In December 63 BCE the consul Cicero had five of Catiline's fellow conspirators, among them the praetor Lentulus, arrested on evidence from Gallic envoys. The senate met in the Temple of Concord to decide their fate, and the consuls-elect and former consuls all spoke for death. Julius Caesar, praetor-elect, argued against it. Sallust, who was not in Rome that year, gives the speech in his own words.
excerpt: All precedents productive of evil effects have had their origin from what was good; but when a government passes into the hands of the ignorant or unprincipled, any new example of severity, inflicted on deserving and suitable objects, is extended to those that are improper and undeserving of it.
source: Sallust, The War with Catiline 51, tr. John Selby Watson, as reprinted in an anthology of orations in 1906. The words are Sallust's composition, not a record of Caesar's.
after: Caesar's call for custody won many senators over until Cato the Younger answered him and carried the senate for death. Cicero had the five executed without trial, announcing 'they have lived'. Catiline was killed at Pistoria early the next year, and in 58 BCE Cicero fled Rome under a law that banished anyone who had executed a citizen without trial.
notes: The article dates the debate to the day after 4 December. Rolfe's Loeb translation on Wikisource (The War With Catiline) is the 1931 edition, so Watson's (in The World's Famous Orations, 1906) was used. The text has one slip of the scan, 'm those' for 'in those' (last paragraph), which a $FIXES entry could mend; the excerpt avoids it.

title: The Sermon on the Mount
speaker: Jesus
before: As the Gospel of Matthew records, early in his preaching in Galilee, after his baptism by John and his temptation in the desert, Jesus saw the crowds, went up a mountain, sat down and began to teach his disciples. It is the first of the five discourses in Matthew. Scholars debate how Matthew composed it: much of the same material is scattered through Luke, whose shorter Sermon on the Plain some take to be the same sermon.
excerpt: Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets.
source: Matthew 5:3-7:27, King James Version (1611), as printed in The Sermon on the Mount (1908).
after: Matthew closes by saying that the crowds were astonished, for he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes. The sermon became a key text of Christian ethics, for Augustine a perfect standard of the Christian life. Leo Tolstoy and Mahatma Gandhi admired it, and it was one of the main sources of Christian pacifism and of the nonviolent American civil rights movement of 1954-1968.
notes: The Gospel gives no date and the article none: display says 1st century CE, and year 30 only places it within the dates of the Jesus entry (c. 4 BCE - c. 30/33 CE). Empire is empty: Galilee was then ruled by the tetrarch Herod Antipas, who has no profile. The imported text is the spoken part (5:3 to 7:27) without Matthew's frame; the 1908 printing is used because Wikisource's Bible (King James) page carries verse numbers, marginal notes and chapter summaries in the text.

title: Al-Hajjaj's Sermon at Kufa
speaker: al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf
before: In early 694 the caliph Abd al-Malik made al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, who had besieged Ibn al-Zubayr in Mecca and then governed the Hejaz, governor of Iraq, the most important post of the Islamic state. Kufa was in disorder: on the death of the last governor the troops of Kufa and Basra serving under al-Muhallab had left their camp and were idling in the cities. Al-Hajjaj gave his inaugural sermon in the mosque.
excerpt: I see before me heads ripe for the sickle, and the reaper—I am he. It seems to me, as if I saw already the blood between your turbans and your shoulders.
source: The opening of the sermon, as translated by Michael Jan de Goeje in the Encyclopaedia Britannica, 11th edition (1911), article Caliphate.
after: He ordered every man who had not returned to the camp within three days to be put to death and his property plundered, and the troops went back. Sent against the Kharijites, they defeated the Azariqa in 696 and another Kharijite leader in 697, but his pay cuts and the unpopular campaigns helped drive the Iraqis into the revolt of Ibn al-Ash'ath in 699, which nearly destroyed Umayyad power in Iraq.
notes: No free English text of the whole sermon was found. De Goeje's paragraph (109 words) is the fullest public-domain English found; Nicholson (A Literary History of the Arabs, 1907, Gutenberg 37985) gives only the opening verse and two sentences, and Muir (The Caliphate, 1891, ch. 50) a paraphrase. The text's 'he said' is the encyclopedist's. The article says only that he was sent in early 694 and then arrived at Kufa: display 694.
